public.title: First Palindromic String
public.source: Find First Palindromic String in the Array (LeetCode 2108)
public.statement: You're given a list of words. Find the first one that reads the same forwards and backwards, and return it. If no word in the list qualifies, return an empty string.
constraints: words[i] is made of lowercase English letters
There may be no palindrome in the list at all

examples.explanation: "ada" is the first word, in order, that reads the same forwards and backwards.
The first word is not a palindrome, so the answer is the second.
No word is a palindrome, so there is nothing to return.

reference_approaches.name: Scan words in order, check each with a two-pointer comparison
sketch: Put one pointer at the start of the word and one at its end, stepping them toward each other and comparing characters as they go
A single mismatched pair disqualifies that word immediately; reaching the middle with every pair matching means it's the answer
reference_approaches.time: O(n times m), n words of length up to m

reference_approaches.name: Scan words in order, check each by reversing and comparing
sketch: Build a reversed copy of the word
Compare that reversed copy to the original word
reference_approaches.space: O(m) per check, for the reversed copy

reference_approaches.name: Collect every palindromic word into a list, then return the first
sketch: Check the palindrome property of every word in the list before deciding anything
Keep each qualifying word in a separate results list as you go
Once the full scan is done, take the first entry of that results list
reference_approaches.time: O(n times m), but never stops early
reference_approaches.space: O(n times m) worst case, for the collected results

reference_approaches.name: Check whether the word's letters could be rearranged into a palindrome
sketch: Count how many times each letter appears within a single word
Treat the word as a match when at most one letter has an odd count

key_insights.text: First means earliest in the list, so check the words in order and return the first palindrome, not the longest one.
hints: If more than one word in the list happens to qualify, which one does the problem actually want back?
Does the order you check the words in matter to the final answer, or only which ones qualify?
Walk the list from the very first word onward, and return the moment one qualifies -- don't look ahead first.

key_insights.text: You can check a word without reversing it by comparing characters from both ends, moving inward.
hints: Do you actually need to build a whole new string to compare against the original, or could you compare characters directly?
What if you looked at the first and last character at the same time, then the second and second-to-last, and so on?
Two positions, one starting at the front and one at the back, stepping toward the middle -- what would that let you check without extra memory?

key_insights.text: Stop checking a word as soon as one pair of characters does not match.
hints: Once you find one pair of characters in a word that don't match each other, do you need to keep checking the rest of that word?
What's the earliest point at which you can be sure a word is NOT a palindrome?
The instant one comparison fails inside a word, that word is done -- you can move on to the next word right away.

key_insights.text: At most a hundred words of a hundred letters, so any correct approach is fast enough.
hints: Given how small the list and the words are allowed to be, how much does the exact approach you pick actually matter for speed?
Roughly how many character comparisons would even the simplest correct approach make, worst case, at these limits?
At a hundred words of a hundred characters each, you're looking at at most about ten thousand character comparisons total either way.

common_wrong_turns.text: Checking whether a word's letters could be rearranged into a palindrome, by counting character frequencies, instead of checking whether the word as written already is one
common_wrong_turns.why_it_fails: A frequency check answers a different question -- whether SOME rearrangement of the letters could be a palindrome -- not whether this exact string, in this exact order, already reads the same forwards and backwards
common_wrong_turns.counter_question: Does the word need to already read the same forwards and backwards as given, or just have letters that could be shuffled into that shape?
common_wrong_turns.failing_case: word = "aabb" -- every letter appears an even number of times, so a frequency check says it could form a palindrome, but "aabb" reversed is "bbaa", which is not equal to "aabb", so it is not actually a palindrome

common_wrong_turns.text: Comparing words at mirrored positions in the array -- the first word to the last, the second to the second-to-last -- instead of checking each word's own characters
common_wrong_turns.why_it_fails: The palindrome property belongs to a single word's own characters, not to that word's position relative to the opposite end of the array, so comparing mirrored array positions checks the wrong thing entirely
common_wrong_turns.counter_question: Whose characters actually need to match each other -- a word's own letters front-to-back, or that word's position against some other word?
common_wrong_turns.failing_case: words = ["abc","car","ada","racecar","cool"] -- comparing the first word "abc" against the last word "cool" tells you nothing about whether "ada", sitting in the middle, is itself a palindrome

common_wrong_turns.text: Assuming the answer should be the longest palindromic word, or the most noticeable one, rather than simply whichever one appears earliest
common_wrong_turns.why_it_fails: The problem defines 'first' strictly by array index -- the earliest qualifying word wins, regardless of its length or how prominent it looks
common_wrong_turns.counter_question: If two different words in the list both qualify, which one does the problem want -- the longer one, or the one that comes first?
common_wrong_turns.failing_case: words = ["ada","racecar"] -- "racecar" is longer, but "ada" comes first, so the correct answer is "ada", not "racecar"

edge_cases: No word in the list is a palindrome, so the empty string must be returned
A single-character word is trivially a palindrome
The list contains only one word
More than one word qualifies -- only the earliest by index counts

followups.question: Your two-pointer check uses no extra memory per word. What would you give up if you used the reverse-and-compare approach instead, and does it actually matter at these constraints?
followups.model_answer: Reversing a word allocates a new string of the same length, so that costs O(m) extra space per check instead of O(1). At these tiny constraints (words up to length one hundred) that's negligible in practice, but the two-pointer version is the one that keeps scaling cleanly if the constraint were much larger.
followups.grading_note: Credit any answer naming the O(1) versus O(m) space tradeoff, even informally.

followups.question: Would your approach notice any slowdown if the list were much larger, and is there a cheaper way to stop once you already have your answer?
followups.model_answer: Collecting every palindromic word before picking the first one does strictly more work than necessary, since it never needs to look past the very first match. Returning as soon as the first qualifying word is found skips checking the rest of the list entirely.
followups.grading_note: Looking for recognition that short-circuiting is available and cheaper, whichever wrong or suboptimal path they took.

followups.question: Walk me through what your approach returns if none of the words in the array are palindromic.
followups.model_answer: It should return the empty string. The scan finishes without ever finding a qualifying word, so the function falls through to a default empty-string return after every word has been checked.
followups.grading_note: Credit any answer that explicitly handles the no-match case by returning an empty string, not null or an error.

private.editorial:
**The move: check each word on its own terms, in the order given.**

The brute-force instinct that actually works here is fine: walk the list, check each word for the palindrome property, and return the first one that qualifies. The interesting part isn't the outer loop -- it's how you check a single word, and being disciplined about what 'first' means.

**Two-pointer scan -- O(n times m) time, O(1) extra space.** For each word, put one index at the front and one at the back, and step them toward the middle, comparing characters as you go. The moment a pair doesn't match, that word is disqualified and you move on; if every pair matches all the way to the middle, that word is your answer. No extra string gets built.

**Reverse-and-compare -- also fine, just costs a little memory.** Building a reversed copy of the word and comparing it to the original works correctly, and at these tiny constraints the extra allocation genuinely doesn't matter. It's a completely reasonable answer; it's just not the version that scales cleanest.

**Why the frequency-check trap is worth naming.** Checking whether a word's letters COULD be rearranged into a palindrome answers a different question than whether the word, exactly as given, already IS one. "aabb" has letter counts that could form a palindrome, but "aabb" itself is not one -- that gap is exactly what trips people up when they pattern-match this problem to a different, similar-sounding one.
